claim: The BOLD contrast was first described by Pauling and Coryell in 1936.
source: The BOLD contrast was first described by Pauling and Coryell, 1936, but it had not been utilized in anesthetized rodent MRI until 1990 (Ogawa et al., 1990a; Ogawa et al., 1990b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pauling and Coryell, 1936

claim: BOLD contrast was not utilized in anesthetized rodent MRI until 1990.
source: The BOLD contrast was first described by Pauling and Coryell, 1936, but it had not been utilized in anesthetized rodent MRI until 1990 (Ogawa et al., 1990a; Ogawa et al., 1990b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ogawa et al., 1990a and 1990b

claim: The power of BOLD-fMRI was revealed in human brain functional mapping.
source: The power of BOLD-fMRI was later revealed in human brain functional mapping (Ogawa et al., 1992; Kwong et al., 1992; Bandettini et al., 1992) and has revolutionized cognitive neuroscience.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ogawa et al., 1992; Kwong et al., 1992; Bandettini et al., 1992

claim: BOLD-fMRI has revolutionized cognitive neuroscience.
source: The power of BOLD-fMRI was later revealed in human brain functional mapping (Ogawa et al., 1992; Kwong et al., 1992; Bandettini et al., 1992) and has revolutionized cognitive neuroscience.
evidence: Based on established scientific consensus about the impact of fMRI on neuroscience

claim: Preclinical fMRI has played a crucial role in method development and validation.
source: In contrast to human studies, preclinical fMRI has played a crucial role in method development and validation (Logothetis et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2016; Yoshida et al., 2016; Pérez-Cervera et al., 2018; Pirttimäki et al., 2016; Arbabi et al., 2022; Labbé et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to preclinical fMRI studies

claim: fMRI of anesthetized rodents reduces confounding artifacts due to motion.
source: fMRI of anesthetized rodents reduces confounding artifacts due to motion and detects robust BOLD or cerebral blood volume signals under various anesthetics (Masamoto et al., 2007; Kawazoe et al., 2022; Bukhari et al., 2018; Steiner et al., 2021; Shim et al., 2018; Jonckers et al., 2014; Tsurugizawa and Yoshimaru, 2021; Bukhari et al., 2017; Grandjean et al., 2014; Becq et al., 2020; Conzen et al., 1992; Magnuson et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2019b; Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to anesthetized rodent fMRI studies

claim: Anesthetized rodent fMRI detects robust BOLD or cerebral blood volume signals under various anesthetics.
source: fMRI of anesthetized rodents reduces confounding artifacts due to motion and detects robust BOLD or cerebral blood volume signals under various anesthetics (Masamoto et al., 2007; Kawazoe et al., 2022; Bukhari et al., 2018; Steiner et al., 2021; Shim et al., 2018; Jonckers et al., 2014; Tsurugizawa and Yoshimaru, 2021; Bukhari et al., 2017; Grandjean et al., 2014; Becq et al., 2020; Conzen et al., 1992; Magnuson et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2019b; Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to anesthetized rodent fMRI studies

claim: The bridging power of preclinical fMRI for basic mechanistic and translational studies has been exploited through combination with genetic modification tools.
source: Recently, the bridging power of preclinical fMRI for basic mechanistic and translational studies has been further exploited given the combination of rodent fMRI with genetic modification tools (e.g. optogenetics, chemogenetics, and genetically encoded biosensors) (Zhou et al., 2023; Jung et al., 2021; Cover et al., 2021; Rocchi et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2022b; Zerbi et al., 2019; Giorgi et al., 2017; Schulz et al., 2012; Ioanas et al., 2022; Jung, 2022; Chen et al., 2019a; Lee et al., 2022a; Nakamura et al., 2020; Peeters et al., 2020; Oyarzabal et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies combining fMRI with genetic tools

claim: Mouse fMRI set a foundation for mechanistic multi-modal imaging in genetic modification models.
source: Among the many efforts in anesthetized rodent fMRI, mouse fMRI set a foundation for mechanistic multi-modal imaging given its global mapping scheme in genetic modification models (Kawazoe et al., 2022; Shim et al., 2018; You et al., 2021; Lake et al., 2020), as well as the ability to perform viral transfections to circuit- or cellular-specific targets in transgenic models.
evidence: Supported by citations to mouse fMRI studies in genetic models

claim: Anesthetics alter brain function during fMRI, preventing accurate interpretation of brain functional changes in awake states.
source: However, anesthetics alter brain function during fMRI, preventing accurate interpretation of brain functional changes in awake states (Masamoto et al., 2007; Jonckers et al., 2014; Grandjean et al., 2014; Conzen et al., 1992; Magnuson et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2020; Sharp et al., 2015; Low et al., 2016a; Gargiulo et al., 2012; Scheller et al., 1988; Crawford et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on anesthetic effects

claim: Awake mouse fMRI provides the most relevant brain functional mapping information for translational cross-scale brain dynamic studies.
source: Awake mouse fMRI presents itself to provide the most relevant brain functional mapping information for translational cross-scale brain dynamic studies.
evidence: Based on inference from the limitations of anesthetized fMRI and the need for translational studies

claim: Surgical implantation of headposts has been developed for head-fixation during awake mouse fMRI.
source: To immobilize the mouse head during scanning, surgical implantation of headposts has been developed for head-fixation similar to optical imaging schemes (Yoshida et al., 2016; Desjardins et al., 2019; Shih et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using headpost implantation

claim: Motion-induced artifacts and potential stress-related issues are major difficulties faced by awake mouse fMRI studies.
source: In contrast to the fMRI mapping of anesthetized animals, motion-induced artifacts and potential stress-related issues caused by loud gradient noises and micro-vibrations during scanning are major difficulties faced by existing awake mouse fMRI studies (Desai et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2020; Gutierrez-Barragan et al., 2022; Han et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020; Almeida et al., 2022; Zeng et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to awake mouse fMRI studies reporting these challenges

claim: Well-planned training procedures can acclimate awake mice during scanning.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that well-planned training procedures could acclimate awake mice during scanning (Han et al., 2019; Madularu et al., 2017b; Xu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020; Almeida et al., 2022; Low et al., 2016b; Chiba et al., 2012; Ferenczi et al., 2016); however, different training paradigms are expected to produce large variability in the functional mapping results (Mandino et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to training studies

claim: Different training paradigms are expected to produce large variability in functional mapping results.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that well-planned training procedures could acclimate awake mice during scanning (Han et al., 2019; Madularu et al., 2017b; Xu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020; Almeida et al., 2022; Low et al., 2016b; Chiba et al., 2012; Ferenczi et al., 2016); however, different training paradigms are expected to produce large variability in the functional mapping results (Mandino et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mandino et al., 2024

claim: Increasing spatiotemporal resolution leads to a reduction in SNR of the images.
source: Since increasing spatiotemporal resolution leads to a reduction in SNR of the images, accessing the highest field MRI available, as well as maximizing the efficiency of the radio frequency (RF) transceiver signal is critical.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of MRI physics

claim: Cryoprobes have been well implemented to boost SNR in MRI.
source: Although cryoprobes have been well implemented to boost SNR (Yoshida et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020; Niendorf et al., 2015), construction limitations of the superconducting environment constrain the usable space and flexibility to accommodate other imaging/recording modalities (Yoshida et al., 2016; Arbabi et al., 2022; Baltes et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2000; Kwok and You, 2006; Takata et al., 2015; Abe et al., 2021; Hamada, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to cryoprobe studies

claim: Construction limitations of the superconducting environment constrain the usable space and flexibility of cryoprobes.
source: Although cryoprobes have been well implemented to boost SNR (Yoshida et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020; Niendorf et al., 2015), construction limitations of the superconducting environment constrain the usable space and flexibility to accommodate other imaging/recording modalities (Yoshida et al., 2016; Arbabi et al., 2022; Baltes et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2000; Kwok and You, 2006; Takata et al., 2015; Abe et al., 2021; Hamada, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies discussing cryoprobe limitations

claim: Implantable coils have been used in animal imaging for over three decades.
source: Implantable coils have been used in animal imaging for over three decades (Pirttimäki et al., 2016; Farmer et al., 1990; Summers et al., 1995; Logothetis et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2018a; Lee et al., 2024; Madularu et al., 2017a; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to implantable coil studies dating back to 1990

claim: Implantable coils gained popularity due to higher SNR and reduction of susceptibility artifacts.
source: Their use gained popularity due to higher SNR and reduction of susceptibility artifacts.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited literature on implantable coils

claim: The main limitation of implantable coils is the need to surgically implant them.
source: The main limitation of implantable coils is the need to surgically implant these coils, adding a degree of invasiveness that MRI usually avoids.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the nature of implantable devices

claim: This study established an awake mouse fMRI platform using an implantable RF surface coil that also functions as a headpost.
source: In this present study, we established an awake mouse fMRI platform by applying an implantable RF surface coil, permanently affixed to the head, which simultaneously functioned as a headpost for fixation during scanning, minimizing animal motion.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's methodology

claim: The implantable RF coil setup allowed acquisition of images with an in-plane spatial resolution of 100 µm and 200 µm slice thickness.
source: This setup allowed us to acquire images with an in-plane spatial resolution of 100 µm and 200 µm slice thickness.
evidence: Direct statement of the imaging parameters achieved

claim: A 5-week training scheme resulted in increased eye movements, presenting decreased struggling and freezing behavior indicative of calmer awake mice during scanning.
source: While there is currently insufficient evidence to ascertain whether head-fixed training leads to stress-free animals, we observed that a 5-week training scheme resulted in increased eye movements, presenting decreased struggling and freezing behavior indicative of calmer awake mice during scanning.
evidence: Based on observations from the training data presented in the study

claim: The implanted RF coil scheme improved B0 homogeneity.
source: This implanted RF coil scheme also improved B0 homogeneity, as well as effectively eliminated any motion-related loading changes causing B1 variability.
evidence: Based on the technical advantages of the implanted coil design

claim: The implanted RF coil scheme effectively eliminated motion-related loading changes causing B1 variability.
source: This implanted RF coil scheme also improved B0 homogeneity, as well as effectively eliminated any motion-related loading changes causing B1 variability.
evidence: Based on the technical advantages of the implanted coil design

claim: The study successfully mapped activated visual and vibrissa pathways in awake mice.
source: Here, we successfully mapped activated visual and vibrissa pathways and detected robust BOLD responses in higher-order association cortices, e.g., anterior cingulate area (ACA) with visual stimulation and ventral retrosplenial area (VRA) with vibrissa stimulation in awake mice based on connectivity map projections from the Allen Brain Atlas derived from a Cre-dependent AAV tracing of axonal projections (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings

claim: Robust BOLD responses were detected in the anterior cingulate area (ACA) with visual stimulation in awake mice.
source: Here, we successfully mapped activated visual and vibrissa pathways and detected robust BOLD responses in higher-order association cortices, e.g., anterior cingulate area (ACA) with visual stimulation and ventral retrosplenial area (VRA) with vibrissa stimulation in awake mice based on connectivity map projections from the Allen Brain Atlas derived from a Cre-dependent AAV tracing of axonal projections (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings

claim: Robust BOLD responses were detected in the ventral retrosplenial area (VRA) with vibrissa stimulation in awake mice.
source: Here, we successfully mapped activated visual and vibrissa pathways and detected robust BOLD responses in higher-order association cortices, e.g., anterior cingulate area (ACA) with visual stimulation and ventral retrosplenial area (VRA) with vibrissa stimulation in awake mice based on connectivity map projections from the Allen Brain Atlas derived from a Cre-dependent AAV tracing of axonal projections (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings

claim: The rapid hemodynamic responses in VRA upon vibrissa stimulation showed a strong correlation with the hippocampus, thalamus, and prefrontal cortical areas.
source: In particular, the rapid hemodynamic responses in VRA upon vibrissa stimulation showed a strong correlation with the hippocampus, thalamus, and prefrontal cortical areas.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings from correlation analysis

claim: Cross-correlation analysis with designated VRA responses revealed early positive BOLD signals at the contralateral barrel cortex (BC) occurring 2 s prior to the air-puff in awake mice with repetitive stimulation.
source: Cross-correlation analysis with designated VRA responses revealed early positive BOLD signals at the contralateral barrel cortex (BC) occurring 2 s prior to the air-puff in awake mice with repetitive stimulation, which was not detected using a randomized stimulation paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings from cross-correlation analysis

claim: Early BC activation was not detected using a randomized stimulation paradigm.
source: Cross-correlation analysis with designated VRA responses revealed early positive BOLD signals at the contralateral barrel cortex (BC) occurring 2 s prior to the air-puff in awake mice with repetitive stimulation, which was not detected using a randomized stimulation paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings comparing repetitive and randomized paradigms

claim: The early BC activation indicated a learned anticipation through the vibrissa system and association cortices in awake mice under continuous exposure of repetitive air-puff stimulation.
source: This early BC activation indicated a learned anticipation through the vibrissa system and association cortices in awake mice under continuous exposure of repetitive air-puff stimulation.
evidence: Interpretation of the early BC activation data

claim: Thirty-eight C57BL/6 mice were used in the current study.
source: Thirty-eight C57BL/6 mice were used in the current study (weighing between 20 g and 30 g) and allocated as follows for each experiment: SNR measurements at 9.4 T – 16 male mice; SNR, visual, and whisker stimulation measurements at 14 T – 13 mice (6F/7M); random stimulation measurements at 14 T – 9 mice (4F/5M).
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental subjects

claim: Mice weighed between 20 g and 30 g.
source: Thirty-eight C57BL/6 mice were used in the current study (weighing between 20 g and 30 g) and allocated as follows for each experiment: SNR measurements at 9.4 T – 16 male mice; SNR, visual, and whisker stimulation measurements at 14 T – 13 mice (6F/7M); random stimulation measurements at 14 T – 9 mice (4F/5M).
evidence: Direct statement of the mouse weights

claim: 16 male mice were used for SNR measurements at 9.4 T.
source: Thirty-eight C57BL/6 mice were used in the current study (weighing between 20 g and 30 g) and allocated as follows for each experiment: SNR measurements at 9.4 T – 16 male mice; SNR, visual, and whisker stimulation measurements at 14 T – 13 mice (6F/7M); random stimulation measurements at 14 T – 9 mice (4F/5M).
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental allocation

claim: 13 mice (6F/7M) were used for SNR, visual, and whisker stimulation measurements at 14 T.
source: Thirty-eight C57BL/6 mice were used in the current study (weighing between 20 g and 30 g) and allocated as follows for each experiment: SNR measurements at 9.4 T – 16 male mice; SNR, visual, and whisker stimulation measurements at 14 T – 13 mice (6F/7M); random stimulation measurements at 14 T – 9 mice (4F/5M).
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental allocation

claim: 9 mice (4F/5M) were used for random stimulation measurements at 14 T.
source: Thirty-eight C57BL/6 mice were used in the current study (weighing between 20 g and 30 g) and allocated as follows for each experiment: SNR measurements at 9.4 T – 16 male mice; SNR, visual, and whisker stimulation measurements at 14 T – 13 mice (6F/7M); random stimulation measurements at 14 T – 9 mice (4F/5M).
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental allocation

claim: Mice were group-housed (3–4/cage) under a 12 hr light/dark cycle with food and water ad libitum.
source: Mice were group-housed (3–4/cage) under a 12 hr light/dark cycle with food and water ad libitum.
evidence: Direct statement of the housing conditions

claim: All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) under protocol number 2020N000073.
source: All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) under protocol number 2020N000073, and animals were cared for according to the requirements of the National Research Council's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: Direct statement of the ethical approval

claim: The awake mouse cradle was designed in Blender and 3D printed using a Formlabs 3L 3D printer.
source: The awake mouse cradle was designed in Blender (Blender Foundation, Amsterdam, NL) and 3D printed using a Formlabs 3L 3D printer (Formlabs Inc, Somerville, MA, USA).
evidence: Direct statement of the design and fabrication method

claim: Two transceiver circuit designs were built: a single loop and a 'figure 8' design.
source: Two transceiver circuit designs were built, a single loop and a 'figure 8' design.
evidence: Direct statement of the coil designs

claim: Each RF coil keeps the B1 direction orthogonal to the B0.
source: Each one keeps the B1 direction orthogonal to the B0.
evidence: Direct statement of the coil design principle

claim: The single loop allows for full brain coverage at sufficient depths for subcortical investigation.
source: The single loop allows for full brain coverage at sufficient depths for subcortical investigation.
evidence: Direct statement of the single loop coil capabilities

claim: The 'figure 8' design is limited to precise measurements of shallow brain regions but provides a significant increase in SNR.
source: The 'figure 8' design, due to its smaller coil loops and B1 direction, is limited to precise measurements of shallow brain regions but provides a significant increase in SNR which is beneficial to cortical-specific studies which do not have a need to look deeper into subcortical regions but would benefit from a much higher SNR.
evidence: Direct statement of the figure 8 coil characteristics

claim: Each coil was built to weigh ~2.5 g minimizing the recovery/neck strengthening time of each mouse.
source: Each coil was built to weigh ~2.5 g minimizing the recovery/neck strengthening time of each mouse.
evidence: Direct statement of the coil weight and its purpose

claim: The coils serve to optimize the B0 homogeneity by minimizing the air-tissue interface.
source: The coils serve to optimize the B0 homogeneity by minimizing the air-tissue interface.
evidence: Direct statement of the coil function

claim: Mice underwent surgery to affix the RF coil to the head.
source: Mice underwent surgery to affix the RF coil to the head.
evidence: Direct statement of the surgical procedure

claim: Animals were anesthetized for surgery using isoflurane.
source: Animals were anesthetized for surgery using isoflurane.

claim: Induction was accomplished using 5% isoflurane and 1 L/min of medical air and 0.2 L/min additional O2 flow.
source: Induction was accomplished using 5% isoflurane and 1 L/min of medical air and 0.2 L/min additional O2 flow.

claim: Animals were maintained at 1.5–2% isoflurane using respiration rate as a monitor for anesthesia depth.
source: Animals were maintained at 1.5–2% isoflurane using respiration rate as a monitor for anesthesia depth.
evidence: Direct statement of the anesthesia maintenance parameters

claim: The coil ring was lifted ~0.3–0.5 mm above the surface of the skull to avoid over-loading effects.
source: The coil ring was lifted ~0.3–0.5 mm above the surface of the skull to avoid over-loading effects and held in place while a thin layer of cyanoacrylate glue was applied to connect the coil to the skull.
evidence: Direct statement of the coil positioning technique

claim: Mice were allowed to recover for at least 1 week to ensure ample neck strengthening had occurred.
source: Mice were then allowed to recover in their home cage for at least 1 week to ensure ample neck strengthening had occurred and the mice could walk with normal head posture.
evidence: Direct statement of the recovery period

claim: Each mouse underwent 5 weeks of intermittent habituation procedures to train animals before fMRI experiments.
source: To acclimate the animals to the MRI environment, each mouse underwent 5 weeks of intermittent habituation procedures to train animals before fMRI experiments by using the following method:
evidence: Direct statement of the training duration

claim: Pupil recordings were measured over 12 training days across 3–4 weeks in Phases 2–4.
source: The pupil recordings were measured over 12 training days across 3–4 weeks in Phases 2–4 (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of the pupil recording schedule

claim: Increased eye movements were well detected in Phase 3 when animals were exposed to the real MRI acoustic noise in the head-fixed position.
source: The increased eye movements were well detected in Phase 3 when animals were exposed to the real MRI acoustic noise in the head-fixed position (located in the RF shielded box attached to the 14 T magnet, i.e. the CCM box) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of the observation from pupil recordings

claim: In Phase 4, animals showed significantly reduced eye movements during the first day when animals were positioned inside the MR scanner with EPI scanning.
source: Interestingly, in Phase 4, animals showed significantly reduced eye movements during the first day when animals were positioned inside the MR scanner with EPI scanning, while an increase in eye movement went back to the level of Phase 3 in the following training days.
evidence: Direct statement of the observation from pupil recordings

claim: The power spectral analysis showed ultra-slow pupil dynamic changes with peaked bandwidths less than 0.02 Hz.
source: The power spectral analysis showed ultra-slow pupil dynamic changes with peaked bandwidths less than 0.02 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement of the spectral analysis results

claim: The power of the ultra-slow pupil dynamics increased as a function of time, particularly during Phase 3.
source: Interestingly, the power of the ultra-slow pupil dynamics also increased as the function of time similar to eye movements, in particular, during Phase 3.
evidence: Direct statement of the observation from spectral analysis

claim: The motion-induced image distortion has been dramatically reduced in well-trained animals compared to the start of in-bore training.
source: Although the actual stress of the animals during scanning remains to be further investigated following the 5-week training procedure, the motion-induced image distortion has been dramatically reduced in well-trained animals compared to the start of in-bore training.
evidence: Direct statement of the training outcome

claim: All animals were anesthetized for the duration of MR scanning during SNR measurements.
source: While acquiring images to measure SNR improvements, all animals were anesthetized for the duration of MR scanning.
evidence: Direct statement of the anesthesia protocol for SNR measurements

claim: Mice were induced using 5% isoflurane in medical air and maintained with 1.0–2.0% isoflurane during SNR measurements.
source: Mice were induced using 5% isoflurane in medical air and maintained with 1.0–2.0% isoflurane, adjusted to retain stable physiological conditions while in the magnet.
evidence: Direct statement of the anesthesia parameters

claim: The animal's breathing rate was continuously monitored and maintained between 50 and 80 breath/min.
source: The animal's breathing rate was continuously monitored and recorded during scanning using a pressure-sensitive sensor-pad and maintained between 50 and 80 breath/min.
evidence: Direct statement of the physiological monitoring

claim: Animals were kept at a constant temperature of 37°C in the MRI scanner.
source: Animals were kept at a constant temperature of 37°C in the MRI scanner by means of blowing warm air through the bore and recorded using a rectal thermometer probe.
evidence: Direct statement of the temperature control

claim: 1H MRI data was acquired using the 14 T and 9.4 T horizontal MRI scanners located at the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging in Boston, MA.
source: 1H MRI data was acquired using the 14 T and 9.4 T horizontal MRI scanners (Magnex Sci, UK) located at the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging in Boston, MA.
evidence: Direct statement of the MRI systems used

claim: The 14 T magnet is equipped with a Bruker Avance Neo Console and is operated using ParaVision 360 V.3.3.
source: The 14 T magnet is equipped with a Bruker Avance Neo Console (Bruker-Biospin, Billerica, MA, USA) and is operated using ParaVision 360 V.3.3.
evidence: Direct statement of the 14 T system specifications

claim: The 14 T microimaging gradient system provides a peak gradient strength of 1.2 T/m over a 60 mm diameter.
source: A microimaging gradient system (Resonance Research, Inc, Billerica, MA, USA) provides a peak gradient strength of 1.2 T/m over a 60 mm diameter.
evidence: Direct statement of the gradient system specifications

claim: The 9.4 T scanner is equipped with a Bruker Avance III HD Console and is operated using ParaVision 6.
source: The 9.4 T scanner is equipped with a Bruker Avance III HD Console (Bruker-Biospin, Billerica, MA, USA) and is operated using ParaVision 6.
evidence: Direct statement of the 9.4 T system specifications

claim: SNR was computed by dividing mean signal over the standard deviation of the noise.
source: SNR was computed by dividing mean signal over the standard deviation of the noise.
evidence: Direct statement of the SNR calculation method

claim: The single loop implantable coils improved SNR over 100% compared to the commercial option at 9.4 T.
source: The single loop implantable coils improved SNR over 100% compared the commercial option while the 'figure 8' style showed a more than five times increase at 9.4 T in the cortical regions.
evidence: Direct statement of the SNR improvement results

claim: The 'figure 8' style coil showed a more than five times increase in SNR at 9.4 T in the cortical regions.
source: The single loop implantable coils improved SNR over 100% compared the commercial option while the 'figure 8' style showed a more than five times increase at 9.4 T in the cortical regions.
evidence: Direct statement of the SNR improvement results

claim: The SNR improvements increased proportionally as a factor of field strength when moving from 9.4 T to 14 T.
source: Moving up to 14 T, the SNR improvements increased proportionally as a factor of field strength (Pohmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement of the SNR scaling with field strength, supported by citation

claim: Multi-slice 2D gradient echo EPI was used to acquire fMRI BOLD data from awake animals with TE/TR = 7 ms/1 s.
source: Multi-slice 2D gradient echo EPI was used to acquire fMRI BOLD data from the awake animals with the following parameters: TE/TR = 7 ms/1 s, segments = 2, bandwidth = 277,777 Hz, 100 µm ×100 µm in plane resolution with a 200 µm slice thickness, 36 slices, 205 repetitions for an acquisition time of 6 min 50 s.
evidence: Direct statement of the fMRI acquisition parameters

claim: The fMRI acquisition used 100 µm × 100 µm in plane resolution with a 200 µm slice thickness.
source: Multi-slice 2D gradient echo EPI was used to acquire fMRI BOLD data from the awake animals with the following parameters: TE/TR = 7 ms/1 s, segments = 2, bandwidth = 277,777 Hz, 100 µm ×100 µm in plane resolution with a 200 µm slice thickness, 36 slices, 205 repetitions for an acquisition time of 6 min 50 s.
evidence: Direct statement of the spatial resolution

claim: The visual stimulation used two different wavelengths of light: 530 nm and 490 nm, which flashed at 5 Hz and 5.1 Hz, respectively, for 8 s.
source: The visual stimulation used two different wavelengths of light: 530 nm and 490 nm, which flashed at 5 Hz and 5.1 Hz, respectively, for 8 s with a 20 ms 'on' time of each illumination.
evidence: Direct statement of the visual stimulation parameters

claim: The whisker air-puff stimulation used a 10 ms puff duration and an 8 Hz firing rate for 8 s.
source: The whisker air-puff stimulation used the same block design as the visual stimulation but was stimulated with a 10 ms puff duration and an 8 Hz firing rate for 8 s.
evidence: Direct statement of the vibrissa stimulation parameters

claim: The stimulation duration resulted in four consecutive scans being included in the 'on' stimulation period and 16 consecutive scans being included in the 'rest' period.
source: Due to the use of two segments for these experiments, the effective TR was 2 s. Therefore, the stimulation duration for both visual and vibrissa experiments resulted in four consecutive scans being included in the 'on' stimulation period and 16 consecutive scans being included in the 'rest' period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of the stimulation timing

claim: The random vibrissa stimulation paradigm used 'rest' durations of 12 s, 22 s, 32 s, and 42 s randomized in three different sequences.
source: The random vibrissa stimulation paradigm used the same 10 ms air-puff at 8 Hz for 8 s but randomized the 'rest' duration. 'Rest' durations were 12 s, 22 s, 32 s, and 42 s and randomized in three different sequences maintaining a scan duration of 205 TRs for each experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of the randomized stimulation parameters

claim: fMRI data was processed using Analysis of Functional Neuroimages (AFNI).
source: fMRI data was processed using Analysis of Functional Neuroimages (AFNI) (Cox, 1996; Cox and Hyde, 1997).
evidence: Direct statement of the analysis software used

claim: A clustering threshold was set at 100 voxels and the Pearson correlation values were limited to p≤0.01 (corrected) with estimated false discover rate at q=0.00078.
source: A clustering threshold was set at 100 voxels and the Pearson correlation values were limited to p≤0.01 (corrected) with estimated false discover rate at q=0.00078.

claim: The implantable RF coil design is based on previously published cable-free (inductive) RF coils.
source: Our design, based on previously published cable-free (inductive) RF coils (Chen et al., 2022), offered an easier pre-scan setup by eliminating the need to localize and secure the pickup coil for inductive coupling optimization.
evidence: Direct statement of the design basis with citation

claim: The current design offered an easier pre-scan setup by eliminating the need to localize and secure the pickup coil for inductive coupling optimization.

source: And while this current design showed reduced freedom for animal movement, implanted coils offer more stable sample loading and reduce the B0 offset when compared to the previous version.

claim: Animal motion can affect B0 homogeneity and cause ghosting if severe enough.
source: As this design was used for awake and minimally restrained mice, the animals would eventually move to adjust themselves (scratching, grooming, teeth grinding, etc.) during the scan. This will affect B0 homogeneity and can cause ghosting if severe enough.
evidence: Direct statement of the motion effects on imaging

claim: Motion artifacts can be minimized through acclimation training which will also reduce unwanted stress.
source: This can be minimized through acclimation training which will also reduce unwanted stress.
evidence: Direct statement of the training benefits

claim: B1 variability was present through motion due to the current design of the coil.
source: Furthermore, B1 variability was present through motion as well due to the current design of the coil.

claim: Body movement could alter the loading of the circuit, inducing B1 artifacts through lifting or dropping the body toward or away from the circuit chip.
source: As the RF circuit chip sits above the animal's neck, body movement could alter the loading of the circuit, inducing B1 artifacts through lifting or dropping the body toward or away from the circuit chip.
evidence: Direct statement of the mechanism of B1 artifacts

claim: Large struggling movements are minimized after the training method.
source: Here, we see that while animal motion still exists (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) large struggling movements are minimized after the training method.
evidence: Direct statement of the training outcome with reference to figure

claim: Mice have a thin skull, which leads to the air-tissue interface being a non-negligible factor at ultra-high fields.
source: Still, mice have a thin skull, which leads to the air-tissue interface being a non-negligible factor at ultra-high fields (e.g. 14 T).
evidence: Based on knowledge of mouse anatomy and MRI physics

claim: The coil implantation reduced the air-tissue interface source of inhomogeneity and allowed for a consistent and stable shim.
source: Therefore, the coil implantation shown here has reduced this source of inhomogeneity (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2) and allowed for a consistent and stable shim.
evidence: Direct statement of the coil implantation benefit with reference to figures

claim: By implanting the coil on the surface of the skull, a significantly higher SNR can be achieved which is comparable to cryoprobe designs at close distances.
source: By implanting the coil on the surface of the skull, we can achieve a significantly higher SNR which can be comparable to cryoprobe designs at close distances.
evidence: Direct statement of the SNR achievement

claim: The 'figure 8' coil gives a five times increase in SNR over the standard commercially available four array mouse head coil for 9.4 T.
source: Moreso, this is the case with the 'figure 8' coil shown in this study which gives a five times increase in SNR over the standard commercially available four array mouse head coil for 9.4 T (both operating at room temperature) (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement of the SNR comparison with reference to figure

claim: This improvement allows much higher spatial resolution in awake mouse fMRI, at a two nanoliter voxel volume, compared to contemporary efforts in human brain mapping at sub-millimeter resolution.
source: This improvement allows much higher spatial resolution in awake mouse fMRI, at a two nanoliter voxel volume, compared to contemporary efforts in human brain mapping at sub-millimeter resolution (0.5–0.8 mm isotropic), a difference of two orders of magnitude (Haenelt et al., 2023; Heidemann et al., 2012; Margalit et al., 2020; Feinberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement of the spatial resolution achievement with citations

claim: Stress remains a confounding factor for brain functional mapping in head-fixed mice despite the extensive training procedure.
source: Despite the extensive training procedure of the present work in comparison to the existing awake mouse fMRI studies (training strategies for awake mice fMRI have been reviewed by Mandino et al., 2024 to show the overall training duration of existing studies), stress remains a confounding factor for the brain functional mapping in head-fixed mice.
evidence: Direct statement of the stress confound with citation

claim: Stress may be related to increased frequency of eye blinking or twitching movements in human subjects.
source: It should be noted that stress may be related to increased frequency of eye blinking or twitching movements in human subjects (Marcos-Ramiro et al., 2014; Haak et al., 2009; Del Carretto and Sessam, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to human studies on stress and eye movements

claim: The eyeblink of head-fixed mice has been used for behavioral conditioning to investigate motor learning in normal behaving mice.
source: However, the eyeblink of head-fixed mice has been used for behavioral conditioning to investigate motor learning in normal behaving mice (Heiney et al., 2014; Chettih et al., 2011; Siegel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to mouse eyeblink conditioning studies

claim: Head-fixed mouse studies have shown that eye movements are significantly reduced compared to free-moving mice.
source: Importantly, head-fixed mouse studies have shown that eye movements are significantly reduced compared to the free-moving mice (Meyer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2020

claim: The increased eye movement during the acclimation process would indicate an alleviated stress level of the head-fixed mice.
source: The increased eye movement during the acclimation process would indicate an alleviated stress level of the head-fixed mice in our cases.
evidence: Interpretation based on the eye movement data and comparison to literature

claim: Stress-related pupillary dilation could dominate the pupil dynamics at the early phase of training.
source: Meanwhile, stress-related pupillary dilation could dominate the pupil dynamics at the early phase of training (Zeng et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2022

claim: A gradually increased pupil dynamic power spectrum at the ultra-slow frequency was observed during Phase 3, presenting alleviated stress-related pupil dilation but recovered pupil dynamics to other factors.
source: We have observed a gradually increased pupil dynamic power spectrum at the ultra-slow frequency during Phase 3, presenting the alleviated stress-related pupil dilation but recovered pupil dynamics to other factors, including arousal, locomotion, startles, etc. in normal behaving mice.
evidence: Direct statement of the observation and interpretation

claim: A recent study shows that the corticosterone concentration in the blood samples of head-fixed mice is significantly reduced on day 25 following the training but remains higher than in the control mice.
source: Nevertheless, a recent study (Juczewski et al., 2020) shows that the corticosterone concentration in the blood samples of head-fixed mice is significantly reduced on day 25 following the training but remains higher than in the control mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Juczewski et al., 2020

claim: The time-dependent changes of stress level during scanning could further confound the functional mapping results if longer than 1 hr.
source: Also, the time-dependent changes of stress level during scanning could further confound the functional mapping results if longer than 1 hr.
evidence: Based on inference about the temporal dynamics of stress

claim: The impact of stress on brain functional mapping with awake mouse fMRI needs further investigation.
source: Thus, the impact of stress on brain functional mapping with awake mouse fMRI would need further investigation, of which the stress-related functional changes should not be neglected from the existing studies.
evidence: Direct statement of the need for further research

claim: There are fMRI studies investigating the visual system in both anesthetized and awake mice.
source: There are fMRI studies investigating the visual system in both anesthetized and awake mice (Dinh et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2022; Huang et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2019; Niranjan et al., 2016; Lungu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to visual system fMRI studies

claim: Robust ACA activation was detected for awake mouse fMRI in this study in contrast to brain activation patterns at the VC, SC, and LGN.
source: In contrast to brain activation patterns at the VC, SC, and LGN (Dinh et al., 2021), robust ACA activation was also detected for awake mouse fMRI in this study (Figure 3).
evidence: Direct statement of the finding with reference to figure and citation

claim: ACA has been closely involved in pupil dynamics, as well as arousal state regulation.
source: Since ACA has been closely involved in pupil dynamics, as well as arousal state regulation (Ebitz and Platt, 2015; Joshi et al., 2016; Pfeffer et al., 2022), the mapping of the ACA in awake mice during visual stimulation provides a meaningful way to validate the conscious state of mice during scanning.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ACA function

claim: The mapping of the ACA in awake mice during visual stimulation provides a meaningful way to validate the conscious state of mice during scanning.
source: Since ACA has been closely involved in pupil dynamics, as well as arousal state regulation (Ebitz and Platt, 2015; Joshi et al., 2016; Pfeffer et al., 2022), the mapping of the ACA in awake mice during visual stimulation provides a meaningful way to validate the conscious state of mice during scanning.
evidence: Inference based on the known function of ACA and the observation of its activation

claim: There are extensive rodent fMRI studies of vibrissa stimulation.
source: Similarly, there are extensive rodent fMRI studies of vibrissa stimulation (You et al., 2021; Van der Knaap et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2004; Balasco et al., 2022; Ferrier et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to vibrissa stimulation fMRI studies

claim: Awake mouse fMRI detected activated contralateral BC and VPM, as well as spread activation in the motor cortex, and small portion of the ipsilateral BC with positive BOLD signals.
source: In contrast to the anesthetized state, this awake mouse fMRI detected not only activated contralateral BC and VPM, but also spread activation in the motor cortex, and small portion of the ipsilateral BC with positive BOLD signals.
evidence: Direct statement of the findings

claim: Videos of the mouse during scanning show that active bilateral whisking could be initiated upon air-puff.
source: Although the air-puff stimulation was set and verified to deflect the whiskers of chosen side, videos of the mouse during scanning show that active bilateral whisking could be initiated upon air-puff.
evidence: Direct statement of the observation from video recordings

claim: Active bilateral whisking could lead to bilateral activation of the motor cortex and the ipsilateral BC.
source: This could lead to bilateral activation of the motor cortex and the ipsilateral BC.
evidence: Inference based on the observed bilateral whisking

claim: Studies have been performed to understand the transcallosal activity-mediated excitatory/inhibitory circuits by both fMRI and optical imaging.
source: Furthermore, studies have been performed to understand the transcallosal activity-mediated excitatory/inhibitory circuits by both fMRI and optical imaging (Chen et al., 2022; Shim et al., 2020; Fujita et al., 2012; Grefkes et al., 2008; Lenzi et al., 2007; Reddy et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcallosal circuit studies

claim: Negative BOLD signals detected across a large brain area are consistent with astrocyte-mediated negative BOLD during brain state changes reported in anesthetized rats.
source: Also, these negative BOLD signals were detected across a large brain area, which is consistent with astrocyte-mediated negative BOLD during brain state changes reported in anesthetized rats (Wang et al., 2018b) and eye open/close-coupled arousal changes in unanesthetized monkeys (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on negative BOLD signals

claim: Astrocytic Ca2+ transients coincide with positive BOLD responses in the activated cortical areas, which align with the neurovascular coupling mechanism.
source: Although astrocytic Ca2+ transients coincide with positive BOLD responses in the activated cortical areas, which align with the neurovascular coupling mechanism (Takata et al., 2018), there is emerging evidence to show that astrocytic Ca2+ transients are coupled with both positive and negative BOLD responses in anesthetized rats (Wang et al., 2018b) and awake mice (Tong et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on astrocytic Ca2+ and BOLD

claim: There is emerging evidence that astrocytic Ca2+ transients are coupled with both positive and negative BOLD responses in anesthetized rats and awake mice.
source: Although astrocytic Ca2+ transients coincide with positive BOLD responses in the activated cortical areas, which align with the neurovascular coupling mechanism (Takata et al., 2018), there is emerging evidence to show that astrocytic Ca2+ transients are coupled with both positive and negative BOLD responses in anesthetized rats (Wang et al., 2018b) and awake mice (Tong et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018b and Tong et al., 2024

claim: Cortex-wide negative BOLD signals coupled with spontaneous astrocytic Ca2+ transients could co-exist with the positive BOLD signal detected at the activated cortex.
source: An intriguing observation is that cortex-wide negative BOLD signals coupled with the spontaneous astrocytic Ca2+ transients could co-exist with the positive BOLD signal detected at the activated cortex.
evidence: Direct statement of the observation

claim: Studies have shown that astrocytes are involved in regulating brain state changes, particularly during locomotion and startle responses.
source: Studies have shown that astrocytes are involved in regulating brain state changes (Poskanzer and Yuste, 2016), in particular, during locomotion (Paukert et al., 2014), and startle responses (Srinivasan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on astrocyte function

claim: Brain state-dependent global negative BOLD responses are related to arousal changes of both non-human primates and human subjects.
source: These brain state-dependent global negative BOLD responses are also related to the arousal changes of both non-human primates (Chang et al., 2016) and human subjects (Setzer et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on arousal and BOLD

claim: Vibrissa stimulation led to robust VRA activation in awake mice.
source: Interestingly, vibrissa stimulation also led to robust VRA activation in awake mice (Radwanska et al., 2010).
evidence: Direct statement of the finding with citation

claim: VRA serves as one of the major nodes of the default mode network across different species.
source: VRA serves as one of the major nodes of the default mode network across different species (Lu et al., 2012; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Vincent et al., 2007; Rilling et al., 2007; Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to default mode network studies

claim: The vibrissa stimulation-evoked VRA activation suggests higher-level cortical function contributes to vibrissa sensory processing in awake mice.
source: The vibrissa stimulation-evoked VRA activation suggests the higher-level cortical function contribute to vibrissa sensory processing in awake mice.
evidence: Inference based on the VRA activation and its known function

claim: There are extensive studies investigating brain activation responsible for anticipation with fMRI and electrophysiological recordings.
source: There are extensive studies investigating brain activation responsible for anticipation with fMRI and electrophysiological recordings (Zhao et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2022; Ploghaus et al., 2003; Sirotin and Das, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to anticipation studies

claim: The repetitive air-puff stimulation delivered during head-fixed training for fMRI studies could serve as a simple paradigm to process the anticipatory responses in awake mice.
source: In contrast to the reward anticipation or audiovisual anticipation of naturalistic music and movie clips that demand more complex cognitive processing (Pezzulo et al., 2007; McRobert et al., 2011; Burton et al., 2009; Ciesielski et al., 2012), the repetitive air-puff stimulation delivered during head-fixed training for fMRI studies could serve as a simple paradigm to process the anticipatory responses in awake mice.
evidence: Inference based on the nature of the stimulation paradigm and comparison to other anticipation studies

claim: The strongest correlation with the BC was detected from 6 s lag-time-based correlation maps, showing a positive BOLD signal at a time point 2 s prior to stimulus onset.
source: Based on cross-correlation analysis with evoked VRA BOLD responses, the strongest correlation with the BC was detected from 6 s lag-time-based correlation maps, showing a positive BOLD signal at a time point 2 s prior to stimulus onset (Figure 5).
evidence: Direct statement of the finding with reference to figure

claim: This anticipatory BC response was not detected when the air-puff stimulation paradigm was randomized in another group of mice.
source: This anticipatory BC response was not detected when the air-puff stimulation paradigm was randomized in another group of mice.
evidence: Direct statement of the control experiment result

claim: VRA is known to be involved in prediction and has been coupled with temporal prediction in rodents.
source: VRA is known to be involved in prediction (Smith et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2019; Auger and Maguire, 2013) and has been coupled with temporal prediction in rodents (Miller et al., 2019; Wyass and Van Groen, 1992), as well as navigation efficiency involving spatial reference cues (Miller et al., 2019; Auger and Maguire, 2013; Wyass and Van Groen, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on VRA function

claim: External somatosensory cues are an important factor when investigating prediction processing.
source: Additionally, external somatosensory cues (e.g. the air-puff or brushing of whiskers) are an important factor when investigating prediction processing (Taube, 2007; Valerio and Taube, 2012; Todd et al., 2019; Cooper et al., 2001; Keene and Bucci, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on prediction processing

claim: Previous work has shown that prediction of external stimulation will cause a hemodynamic response even in the absence of a stimulus.
source: Previous work has shown that prediction of external stimulation will cause a hemodynamic response even in the absence of a stimulus (Sirotin and Das, 2009; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sirotin and Das, 2009 and Yu et al., 2019

claim: After continued regularly spaced stimulation, early somatosensory hemodynamic responses begin to have a significant impact seen in the averaged BOLD response time course.
source: In our study, we show that after continued regularly spaced stimulation, early somatosensory hemodynamic responses begin to have a significant impact seen in the averaged BOLD response time course.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's finding

claim: These anticipatory hemodynamic responses are a result of the continuous training for mice experiencing months of repetitive stimulation.
source: These anticipatory hemodynamic responses are a result of the continuous training for mice experiencing months of repetitive stimulation.
evidence: Inference based on the training duration and the observed responses

claim: The increased BOLD signal in the BC before the stimulus onset shows strong cross-correlation to the VRA activation.
source: The increased BOLD signal in the BC before the stimulus onset shows strong cross-correlation to the VRA activation, but VRA activation is not dependent on the pre-stimulus activation in the BC.
evidence: Direct statement of the correlation analysis result

claim: VRA activation is not dependent on the pre-stimulus activation in the BC.
source: The increased BOLD signal in the BC before the stimulus onset shows strong cross-correlation to the VRA activation, but VRA activation is not dependent on the pre-stimulus activation in the BC.
evidence: Direct statement of the independence of VRA activation

claim: Comparable VRA BOLD responses were observed between repetitive and randomized air-puff stimulation paradigms.
source: This can be seen through the comparable VRA BOLD responses between repetitive and randomized air-puff stimulation paradigms (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement of the comparison with reference to figure

claim: VRA response mediates external sensory perception and may serve as a key association cortical area for the processing of the anticipated vibrissa signals.
source: This result indicates that VRA response mediates external sensory perception and may serve as a key association cortical area for the processing of the anticipated vibrissa signals but is not solely dependent on the prediction of incoming stimulus.
evidence: Inference based on the VRA activation patterns and correlation analysis

claim: VRA is not solely dependent on the prediction of incoming stimulus.
source: This result indicates that VRA response mediates external sensory perception and may serve as a key association cortical area for the processing of the anticipated vibrissa signals but is not solely dependent on the prediction of incoming stimulus.
evidence: Inference based on the comparable VRA responses in both paradigms

claim: The single loop implantable coils improved SNR significantly up to 4 mm depth compared to the phase-array coil at 9.4 T.
source: The SNR along the dorsal-ventral axis was plotted to compare the B1 field sensitivity of the single loop and 'figure 8' RF coils in comparison with the phase-array coil at 9.4 T, showing significantly increased SNR up to 4 mm depth (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1B showing the SNR profile

claim: The EPI-based T2* images acquired from head-fixed awake mice show little air-tissue interface-induced image distortion.
source: The EPI-based T2* images acquired from head-fixed awake mice show little air-tissue interface-induced image distortion with the same spatial resolution as anatomical images (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2C and D showing the image quality

claim: Motion artifacts were detected at some time points of the fMRI time course, presenting large EPI image distortions.
source: Motion artifacts were detected at some time points of the fMRI time course, presenting large EPI image distortions (Figure 3E, Video 2), but can be removed using a censoring function during data analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3E and Video 2 showing motion artifacts

claim: Motion artifacts can be removed using a censoring function during data analysis.
source: Motion artifacts were detected at some time points of the fMRI time course, presenting large EPI image distortions (Figure 3E, Video 2), but can be removed using a censoring function during data analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing the censoring method

claim: Brain-wide functional maps using the visual stimulation paradigm showed activated areas along the visual pathways including VC, SC, LGN, and ACA.
source: Brain-wide functional maps using the visual stimulation paradigm were seen with activated areas highlighted along the visual pathways (Figure 3). These areas included the visual cortex (VC), superior colliculus (SC), lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), and association cortex in the ACA.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3 showing the activation maps

claim: The activated barrel cortex (BC) and ventroposterior medial nucleus (VPM) were seen related to stimulation of the contralateral whisker pad.
source: The activated barrel cortex (BC) and ventroposterior medial nucleus (VPM) were seen related to stimulation of the contralateral whisker pad (time courses in Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing the activation

claim: Brain-wide functional maps showed activation in the motor cortex and a small portion of the ipsilateral BC during vibrissa stimulation.
source: Brain-wide functional maps also showed activation in the motor cortex and a small portion of the ipsilateral BC.
evidence: Direct statement of the functional mapping results

claim: At a zero time shift, the VRA is strongly correlated with the hippocampus, cingulate cortex, and central thalamic regions.
source: At a zero time shift (map developed from peak BOLD response), the VRA is strongly correlated with the hippocampus, cingulate cortex, and central thalamic regions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5A showing the correlation map

claim: At a –6 s time shift, stronger correlation was observed at the contralateral BC, indicating anticipation of the repetitive air-puff in the block design.
source: Nevertheless, at a –6 s time shift (i.e. 2 s before stimulation onset), stronger correlation was observed at the contralateral BC, indicating anticipation of the repetitive air-puff in the block design (Figure 5A).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5A showing the correlation map at -6s

claim: VRA remained strongly coupled with other association cortices and subcortical regions at the zero time shift in the randomized stimulation group.
source: Although VRA remained strongly coupled with the other association cortices and subcortical regions at the zero time shift, no correlation was observed from the contralateral BC at the –6 s time shift (Figure 5B).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5B showing the correlation map

claim: No correlation was observed from the contralateral BC at the –6 s time shift in the randomized stimulation group.
source: Although VRA remained strongly coupled with the other association cortices and subcortical regions at the zero time shift, no correlation was observed from the contralateral BC at the –6 s time shift (Figure 5B).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5B showing the absence of correlation

claim: The fMRI time course analysis from the contralateral BC showed increased BOLD responses before the air-puff in the block design group, but not the randomized control group.
source: The fMRI time course analysis from the contralateral BC also showed increased BOLD responses before the air-puff in the block design group, but not the randomized control group (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5C showing the time course comparison

claim: Quantitative analysis showed a significantly higher BOLD signal 2 s before the air-puff stimulation in the standard block design group when compared with the randomized group.
source: Quantitative analysis showed a significantly higher BOLD signal 2 s before the air-puff stimulation in the standard block design group when compared with the randomized group (Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5D showing the quantitative comparison

claim: VRA responses between the two groups (repetitive and randomized) were similar.
source: It should be noted that VRA responses between the two groups were similar, further confirming the anticipation-related early BC activation to repetitive air-puff stimulation.
evidence: Direct statement of the comparison result
